title_fr: Analyse des opérations M&A & levée de fonds du 12 septembre 2026
title_en:
M&A & Fundraising Analysis for September 12, 2026

SUBTITLE===
New space, carbon footprint, vertical software, and charging infrastructure: European capital is repositioning itself on what cannot be dematerialized — a complete daily overview for decision-makers and investors.

===BODY===
Space and energy structured the fundraising side today, while vertical software and industrial automation concentrated M&A movements. France occupies an unusual space: between a European record in new space, an accelerated consolidation of regulatory carbon footprints, and discreet but methodical external growth operations in engineering and healthcare. In Europe, two take-privates of listed software companies in England signal that public markets continue to undervalue what private equity is willing to pay.

# 🤝 M&A Transactions

## KEBA acquires Transtechnik: When industrial automation is bought through a trusted network

**KEBA**, an Austrian group specializing in industrial automation, acquires **Transtechnik SAS**, a Dijon-based integrator founded in 1987, active in cosmetics, packaging, and agri-food. Amount not disclosed.

The immediate interpretation: an international player strengthening its commercial presence in France, a market considered strategic for automation in Europe.

*What is really at play is more subtle: Transtechnik is not a distributor; it is a project engineering firm that supports its clients throughout an industrial cycle — from consulting to commissioning. What KEBA is buying is less a order book than a thirty-five-year-old relationship of trust with demanding clients. In a market where French industrialists are hesitant to entrust their transformation to a foreign supplier without local roots, this relational depth is precisely what cannot be built quickly.* For a European automation player looking to establish itself in France, the shortest path is often to acquire someone who already knows the customers.

## Caudalie Group acquires Talm: The first acquisition by a house that never made any

**Caudalie Group**, founded by Mathilde and Bertrand Thomas, acquires **Talm**, a young Parisian cosmetics brand founded five years ago by Kenza Keller. Amount not disclosed.

For Caudalie, this is a first: the group had never before acquired an external brand. The operation was built on the continuity of a personal relationship between founders — Kenza Keller was looking for accelerated distribution, Caudalie was looking to broaden its spectrum without diluting its identity.

*This type of founder-to-founder acquisition in premium cosmetics works when the seller chooses their acquirer as much as the other way around. Distribution is the real asset Talm is buying here — not a check, but access to a retail network and international infrastructure that five years of organic growth would not have been enough to build.* For emerging brands in the sector, the operation is a reminder that an exit to a family group aligned with their values can be worth more, in the long run, than an additional fundraising round.

## TotalEnergies buys back Plastic Energy's 35% stake in Grandpuits: Industrial sovereignty before profitability

**TotalEnergies** increases its stake in the **Grandpuits** (Seine-et-Marne) chemical recycling plant to 100%, after acquiring the share held by the British company **Plastic Energy**, as part of the latter's capital restructuring. The plant, which started operations in March 2026, processes 15,000 tons of plastic waste per year through pyrolysis.

The obvious interpretation: TotalEnergies consolidates a symbolically strong industrial asset — the conversion of an oil site into recycling infrastructure — and simplifies its governance.

*The important detail lies in the circumstances: it was Plastic Energy's restructuring that made the sale possible, not an offensive strategic decision by TotalEnergies. The group therefore regains full control of an asset whose capacity represents less than 0.3% of household packaging placed on the French market — a symbolic volume in the face of criticism about the energy-intensive nature of the process. What TotalEnergies is buying here is primarily complete control of an industrial showcase at a time when European regulations on recycled plastics will create captive demand.* The question is not the immediate profitability of Grandpuits — it is whether the group will be in a position to scale up when regulations make this outlet mandatory.

## Qualitas Energy acquires Cero Generation's European platform: 5.8 GW change hands

**Qualitas Energy** acquires **Cero Generation**'s European platform, previously owned by **Macquarie Group**, via its Qualitas Energy Fund VI. The portfolio covers 5.8 GW spread across the United Kingdom, Italy, and Spain — including over 2 GW in operation, construction, or ready-to-build, and 3.8 GW in the development pipeline. Amount not disclosed.

Cero was created in 2021 by Macquarie as a vehicle dedicated to solar PV and battery energy storage systems (BESS). It retains its teams and offices in London, Milan, and Madrid under the Cero brand.

*What Macquarie is selling is development pipeline as much as assets in production — and that is precisely what Qualitas is paying for: the ability to transform 3.8 GW of construction rights into future cash flows. In renewable energy, the real competitive advantage is no longer knowing how to build solar panels; it is controlling authorized land and grid connections in markets where permits are becoming scarce.* For a player like Qualitas, acquiring a pipeline of this size in three markets where it was already present is a way to buy ten years of organic development in a single transaction.

# 🚀 Fundraisings

## The Exploration Company raises $450 million: European new space tests its maturity

**The Exploration Company (TEC)**, founded in 2021 by Hélène Huby, closes a **$450 million Series C** (~**€414 million**), a European record for a space company at this stage. The fundraising brings the company's cumulative funding to approximately $680 million since its creation. Following this, the European Space Agency awards TEC a **€760 million** service contract for the next phase of the European reusable space cargo program. TEC develops the Nyx capsule at three sites: Munich (headquarters), Le Haillan near Bordeaux, and Turin.

The immediate interpretation: a Franco-German startup establishing itself as a European new space champion, supported by Macron and Von der Leyen at the Paris summit.

*Two elements deserve to be separated. First, the fundraising: at this stage of development, $450 million primarily finances heavy physical capital — engines, test infrastructure, assembly lines — with still modest teams. This is the financial structure of an industry, not software: almost all the money goes into machines and engineering, very little into payroll proportionally. This is not a flaw; it is the nature of the space sector. Second, the ESA contract: €760 million in guaranteed revenue over several years means public demand retroactively validates private infrastructure — exactly the mechanism that allowed SpaceX to survive its early years.* For European investors in industrial deep tech, TEC illustrates that the "sovereign contract + private capital" model can work without relying exclusively on NASA or the Pentagon.

## Logivolt raises €300 million: Funding charging stations or funding a network?

**Logivolt** obtains a **€300 million green loan** via the **BPCE** group to deploy 1.7 million residential charging points by 2030.

The obvious interpretation: supporting the rise of electric vehicles, which now account for 35% of new registrations.

*The real issue is in the physics of the network, not in finance. 1.7 million residential charging stations connected simultaneously between 7 PM and 11 PM represent a load that, according to operator estimates, could be equivalent to several nuclear reactors during peak hours. The question that this funding does not solve — and that no one directly asks — is that of intelligent load management: without active coordination between charging stations, neighborhood transformers become the bottleneck. What Logivolt is actually funding is as much a network infrastructure problem as a charging station problem.* For local authorities and network managers, the challenge is not the number of charging stations installed but the ability to modulate their power demand — and that is where the true value of the deployment will lie.

## Mistral raises €105 million from European investors: The political signal behind the funding round

**Mistral AI** closes a **€105 million** round, fully subscribed by European investors, in a context where its main €3 billion fundraising (announced in dominant news) marks a turning point for the French ecosystem.

The operation is presented as a signal of digital sovereignty: demonstrating that Europe can finance its own foundation models without relying on American or Asian capital.

*What is interesting about this specific round — distinct from the main fundraising — is precisely its composition: 100% European in a market where large American funds are actively seeking to take positions in AI labs. This is not a coincidence of timing; it is a deliberate demonstration of the continent's ability to finance its own artificial intelligence infrastructure. The real question remains open: the sovereignty of the model depends as much on the compute it runs on as on the identity of the shareholders.* For French companies evaluating their AI options, Mistral's rise as a fully funded player concretely changes the make-or-buy equation.

## Greenly acquires Normative and Watershed: Regulatory consolidation accelerates

**Greenly** simultaneously announces two acquisitions: **Normative**, a Swedish carbon footprint player valued in an operation described at **€75 million**, and **Watershed**, a British player in the sector (amount not disclosed, operation valued at approximately **€52 million** according to sources). This brings Greenly to over 4,000 clients in more than 30 countries.

Both operations respond to the same logic: the CSRD directive will require some 50,000 European companies with more than 250 employees to publish a complete and audited carbon footprint by 2028.

*What changes with the CSRD is the very nature of the market: the carbon footprint ceases to be a voluntary tool and becomes a legal, audited obligation. In this context, fragmentation — four or five different tools depending on subsidiaries, scopes, and standards — becomes a compliance risk, not just an operational inconvenience. Greenly is not buying competitors to eliminate them: it is buying emissions databases, scientific methodologies (Normative), and industrial integration teams (Watershed, 35 engineers). What the market will pay for tomorrow is the platform that covers Scope 1, 2, and 3 in a single auditable environment.* For CSR and CFOs of groups affected by the CSRD, market consolidation means that the tool choice made today will likely commit them for five years.

## Galeon refuses €60 million and raises €6 million: Refusal as a strategic signal

**Galeon**, an Annecy-based publisher of AI-native patient records, refuses a **€60 million** acquisition offer and instead raises **€6 million** from its community of hospital pioneers and **BPI France**. The company equips 19 hospitals, employs about forty people, and aims for profitability by the end of 2027.

*The refusal is the real information. At €60 million, the potential acquirer valued a niche publisher. By refusing, Galeon bets that the sovereignty of health data — HDS-certified hosting in France, beyond the reach of extra-European legislation — will become a decisive selection criterion for public hospitals, and that this sovereignty premium is not yet integrated into the offered price. The €6 million raised from the hospitals themselves — clients who become shareholders — creates a community of interests that complicates any unwanted future acquisition.* This is a form of capital defense as much as growth financing.

## Arlequin AI raises €28 million in Series A: Topology where large models fail

**Arlequin AI** closes a **€28 million Series A**, co-led by the Polish fund **OTB Ventures** and **Redalpine**, with the participation of **BPI France**'s Defense Innovation Fund, **Xavier Niel**, and the accelerator **ZEBOX** (CMA CGM). The startup, founded in 2024, develops topological neural networks to detect hidden structures behind money laundering, terrorist financing, and disinformation.

Where large language models analyze text and statistical patterns, Arlequin's technology maps networks of relationships — who funds whom, who communicates with whom, which seemingly unrelated entities share a common structure. The HuDEx platform is already commercially operating with governments and large organizations in Europe.

*The funding by BPI's Defense Innovation Fund and the presence of CMA CGM (via ZEBOX) are two distinct signals: the first validates sovereign and governmental use, the second points to the fight against fraud in maritime logistics chains — a considerable market. A 50-person startup with 35 engineers and 15 PhD researchers, founded in 2024 and already in commercial deployment, is an execution pace that explains the interest of a fund the size of OTB for such an early-stage asset.* For financial compliance and security players, network topology is a blind spot that traditional tools do not cover — and it is precisely this gap that this fundraising finances.

## Wheere aims for €140 million for a geolocation constellation: Fundraising as a two-step process

**Wheere**, a Montpellier-based spacetech specializing in indoor and outdoor satellite geolocation, announces its aim to raise **€140 million** by the end of 2028: €40 million in France in the second half of 2027, then €100 million in the United States. The goal: to orbit 65 satellites and address the mass market from 2030-2032.

The company emerges from the International Space Summit with a first commercial contract for its terrestrial technology and a target of €1 million in revenue this year.

*What is notable here is the transparency of the financing timeline and geography: the co-founder publicly announces that he is going to San Francisco to seek the missing €100 million after an initial French tranche. This is an admission as much as a strategy — the European space venture market is not yet sufficient to solely finance a constellation, even a modest one. Validation by the ecosystem (CNES, ESA, NASA, SpaceX) at the Paris summit is presented as a necessary prerequisite for fundraising, not a consequence.* For French investors looking at new space, Wheere illustrates the structural challenge: initial tranches are raised in Europe, but subsequent ones almost systematically require a pivot to American capital.

## JL&P raises €22 million in debt and acquires EGEH: Methodical external growth in engineering

**JL&P**, a Gironde-based engineering and architecture group based in Floirac, raises **€22 million** in debt from a banking pool (Crédit Agricole, LCL, BNP Paribas, Crédit Mutuel), including €16 million in confirmed credit lines. Following this, the group announces the acquisition of **EGEH**, a specialist in polluted sites and soils, hydrogeology, and water law, with teams in Limoges, Floirac, Nantes, and Île-de-France. Amount not disclosed. JL&P has been supported by **Swen Capital Partners** and **Arkéa Capital** as minority shareholders since 2024.

*The operation illustrates a disciplined regional build-up model: debt is raised before it is needed, and the confirmed credit line provides the ability to act quickly on subsequent targets. EGEH brings regulatory expertise (water law, polluted soils) that is becoming increasingly critical as environmental constraints on industrial and real estate projects intensify.* For mid-sized environmental engineering players, the signal is clear: consolidation is underway, and independent firms well-positioned in regulatory niches are attractive targets.

## Accel-KKR acquires Eleco for £207.6 million: The exit premium from the listed market

**Accel-KKR** launches a takeover bid for **Eleco**, a British group listed on AIM specializing in software for construction, for **£207.6 million** (~**€243 million**), representing a premium of 74.7% over the last closing price before the announcement and 89.9% over the weighted average of the last six months. The operation is fully financed by Accel-KKR's equity, without debt.

*The 75% premium is the figure worth noting. It does not mean that Eleco was undervalued: it means that the listed market applied a structural discount to this type of asset — niche vertical software, low liquidity, the construction market perceived as cyclical. Accel-KKR pays 20 times EBITDA for mission-critical software whose customers do not easily switch solutions. By taking Eleco private, the fund buys the freedom to invest in growth without having to justify a margin trajectory to dispersed shareholders every quarter.* The take-private here is less a conviction about Eleco than an arbitrage between two valuation markets: private equity pays more, but it buys time.

## Main Capital Partners acquires Tribal Group for £189.3 million: Educational software as a sovereign asset

**Main Capital Partners**, a software-focused fund managing approximately €12 billion in assets, acquires **Tribal Group**, a British publisher of mission-critical software for international higher education, for approximately **£189.3 million** (~**€221 million**). Tribal was listed on AIM. The operation takes the form of an asset sale requiring shareholder vote.

Tribal provides information systems to universities and educational institutions internationally — tools on which institutions rely to manage registrations, results, and regulatory compliance.

*Second listed software take-private in one day, same underlying logic: an asset whose value lies in criticality and customer stickiness — a university does not change its information system from one year to the next — but whose listed market cannot adequately value recurrence. Main Capital specializes in B2B software in Europe; for them, Tribal is a building block in a broader thesis of consolidating vertical tools for higher education.* The signal for IT departments of affected institutions: their supplier will now operate under the pressure of a five-to-seven-year valuation horizon, with a growth and margin trajectory to maintain.

## Hardloop: Founders regain majority via a secondary LBO

**Hardloop**, an e-commerce platform for outdoor equipment based in Annecy, welcomes **iX Private Equity** to its capital in an operation that allows co-founders Guillaume Richard and Julien Jérémie to increase their stake from 49.6% to nearly 60%. The operation coincides with the exit of 21 historical investors (Seventure, SGPA, Kima Ventures, angels). Amount not disclosed; the company is valued at approximately **€100 million** according to sources. Hardloop exceeds €40 million in revenue with 34% growth in 2026.

*The structure is unusual: the founders emerge strengthened from a liquidity event, which is generally the opposite of what happens in a classic secondary LBO. iX Private Equity agreed to finance the liquidity of former investors while allowing the founders to take majority control — a sign that the investment thesis relies entirely on managerial continuity. In a consolidating outdoor market, Hardloop aims for €100 million in revenue in three years: the fund bets that the platform can double without changing its management team.* For entrepreneurs in the secondary LBO phase, this is a negotiation model to remember: continuity can be monetized in terms of governance.

## Francisco Partners and KKR take minority stakes in TeamSystem: "Private IPO" as a substitute exit

**Francisco Partners** acquires approximately 10% of **TeamSystem**, an Italian publisher of management software (accounting, payroll, ERP) from **Hellman & Friedman**, while **KKR** and other investors take an additional 5%. The implied valuation of TeamSystem is between €8 billion and €10 billion. H&F retains the rest of its stake, transferred to a new fund.

*The operation illustrates a mechanism that is spreading in Europe: the "private IPO," or how a fund returns capital to its LPs without going through public markets. In a context where IPOs are difficult for large software companies — markets have been shaken by fears about the impact of AI on valuations — H&F partially liquidates a €8-10 billion position without exposing TeamSystem to the volatility of a free float. Francisco Partners and KKR enter at a valuation that, at this level, implies a strong conviction about the ability of vertical management software to resist substitution by AI — or to integrate it as a growth driver.* For funds holding similar-sized software assets in Europe, TeamSystem validates that the private secondary market can absorb significant blocks without a major liquidity discount.

## HVR Energy raises €20 million for 75 hydrogen stations in Spain

**HVR Energy**, a Spanish operator of hydrogen charging stations, closes a **€20 million Series A**, led by **Sandton** (€15 million), with **Barents Re** (€3 million) and **Langur** (€2 million). The pre-money valuation is €100 million. The goal: 75 stations in Spain by 2030, after a first opening in Coslada in 2023.

Hydrogen for heavy mobility remains an infrastructure under construction: European AFIR and RED III regulations create a deployment obligation, but effective commercial demand depends on the speed at which hydrogen vehicle fleets develop.

*HVR Energy's real risk is not financial but temporal: building the infrastructure before vehicles arrive is costly, but waiting for vehicles to arrive before building the infrastructure creates a circular blockage. The €20 million serves precisely to take this timing risk — betting that regulation will force demand before capital is exhausted.* For investors in alternative mobility, it's the same equation as with electric charging ten years ago, with a longer risk window.

## HeyDiga raises €5.5 million to automate inbound calls for SMEs

**HeyDiga**, a Madrid-based startup founded in July 2025, closes a **€5.5 million seed round** led by **6 Degrees Capital** (London), with **K Fund**, **Italian Founders Fund**, and **Decelera**. The company deploys AI conversational agents on phone, WhatsApp, and chat for small and medium-sized enterprises, and claims 78% of conversations handled without human intervention for 200 clients.

Founded fourteen months ago, HeyDiga has already raised approximately €6.5 million in total. Traction is real in specific verticals — automotive, catering — where the volume of inbound calls is high and the need for personalization is limited.

*The addressed market is immense but very fragmented: convincing thousands of SMEs to adopt such a tool, one by one, is as much a distribution problem as a product problem. The €5.5 million will likely finance sales force as much as the product itself.* To watch: the ability to build indirect distribution channels (integrators, sectoral platforms) rather than selling directly.

===WHYS===
1. The acquirer seeks to consolidate their political positioning and broaden their electoral base after their recent record donation.
2. Their complementary electoral base and political positioning would significantly expand their reach and influence after their recent donation.
3. The acquirer seeks to expand their AI expertise in industrial procurement, a logical follow-up to their recent operation.
4. Their AI assistant for SMEs without a dedicated purchasing team complements their focus on the AI revolution.
5. The acquirer seeks to consolidate their presence in France and extend their automation solutions to energy systems.
6. Their expertise in custom transformers and inductors would complement their industrial automation offering, a logical follow-up to the integration of Transtechnik.

La France occupe un espace inhabituel : entre un record européen dans le new space, une consolidation accélérée du bilan carbone réglementaire, et des opérations de croissance externe discrètes mais méthodiques dans l'ingénierie et la santé. En Europe, deux take-privates de logiciels cotés en Angleterre signalent que les marchés publics continuent de sous-valoriser ce que le private equity est prêt à payer.

    Greenly acquiert Normative et Watershed : la consolidation réglementaire s'accélère

    Source : esgtoday.com → · Secteur Horizontal & Productivity SaaS — 📬 s'abonner à la newsletter Horizontal & Productivity SaaS

    Greenly annonce simultanément deux acquisitions : Normative, acteur suédois du bilan carbone valorisé dans une opération décrite à 75 millions d'euros, et Watershed, acteur britannique du secteur (montant non communiqué, opération valorisée à environ 52 millions d'euros selon les sources). L'ensemble porte Greenly à plus de 4 000 clients dans plus de 30 pays.

    Les deux opérations répondent à la même logique : la directive CSRD imposera d'ici 2028 à quelque 50 000 entreprises européennes de plus de 250 salariés de publier un bilan carbone complet et audité.

    Ce qui change avec la CSRD, c'est la nature même du marché : le bilan carbone cesse d'être un outil volontaire pour devenir une obligation légale auditée. Dans ce contexte, la fragmentation — quatre ou cinq outils différents selon les filiales, les périmètres, les référentiels — devient un risque de conformité, pas seulement un inconfort opérationnel. Greenly ne rachète pas des concurrents pour les éliminer : il rachète des bases de données d'émissions, des méthodologies scientifiques (Normative) et des équipes d'intégration industrielle (Watershed, 35 ingénieurs). Ce que le marché paiera demain, c'est la plateforme qui couvre Scope 1, 2 et 3 dans un seul environnement auditable. Pour les directions RSE et les DAF des groupes concernés par la CSRD, la consolidation du marché signifie que le choix d'outil fait aujourd'hui engage probablement pour cinq ans.

    Caudalie Group acquiert Talm, jeune pousse parisienne de cosmétiques

    Rachat / M&AFrance

    Caudalie Group acquiert Talm : la première acquisition d'une maison qui n'en faisait jamais

    Source : fr.fashionnetwork.com →

    Caudalie Group, fondé par Mathilde et Bertrand Thomas, acquiert Talm, jeune marque de cosmétiques parisienne fondée il y a cinq ans par Kenza Keller. Montant non communiqué.

    Pour Caudalie, c'est une première : le groupe n'avait jusqu'ici jamais acquis de marque extérieure. L'opération s'est construite dans la continuité d'une relation personnelle entre fondateurs — Kenza Keller cherchait une accélération sur la distribution, Caudalie cherchait à élargir son spectre sans diluer son identité.

    Ce type d'acquisition fondateur-à-fondateur dans la cosmétique premium fonctionne quand le vendeur choisit son acquéreur autant que l'inverse. La distribution est le vrai actif que Talm achète ici — non un chèque, mais l'accès à un réseau retail et à une infrastructure internationale que cinq ans de croissance organique n'auraient pas suffi à construire. Pour les marques émergentes du secteur, l'opération rappelle qu'une sortie vers un groupe familial aligné sur les valeurs peut valoir plus, à terme, qu'une levée de fonds supplémentaire.

    Rachat / M&AFrance

    KEBA absorbe Transtechnik : quand l'automatisation industrielle s'achète en réseau de confiance

    Source : bprfrance.com → · Secteur B2B Software & Cloud — 📬 s'abonner à la newsletter B2B Software & Cloud

    KEBA, groupe autrichien spécialisé en automatisation industrielle, acquiert Transtechnik SAS, intégrateur dijonnais fondé en 1987, actif dans la cosmétique, l'emballage et l'agroalimentaire. Montant non communiqué.

    La lecture immédiate : un acteur international qui densifie sa présence commerciale en France, marché jugé stratégique pour l'automatisation en Europe.

    Ce qui se joue réellement est plus fin : Transtechnik n'est pas un distributeur, c'est un bureau d'ingénierie de projet qui accompagne ses clients sur toute la durée d'un cycle industriel — du conseil à la mise en service. Ce que KEBA achète, c'est moins un carnet de commandes qu'une relation de confiance installée sur trente-cinq ans avec des donneurs d'ordre exigeants. Dans un marché où les industriels français hésitent à confier leur transformation à un fournisseur étranger sans ancrage local, cette profondeur relationnelle est précisément ce qu'on ne peut pas construire vite. Pour un acteur européen de l'automatisation qui cherche à s'implanter en France, la voie la plus courte reste souvent de racheter celui qui connaît déjà les clients.

    Qualitas acquires Cero’s European platform from Macquarie

    Rachat / M&AEurope

    Qualitas Energy acquiert la plateforme européenne de Cero Generation : 5,8 GW changent de main

    Source : evertiq.com →

    Qualitas Energy acquiert la plateforme européenne de Cero Generation, jusqu'ici détenue par Macquarie Group, via son fonds Qualitas Energy Fund VI. Le portefeuille couvre 5,8 GW répartis au Royaume-Uni, en Italie et en Espagne — dont plus de 2 GW en opération, construction ou prêts à construire, et 3,8 GW en pipeline de développement. Montant non communiqué.

    Cero a été créée en 2021 par Macquarie comme véhicule dédié au solaire PV et au stockage par batteries (BESS). Elle conserve ses équipes et ses bureaux à Londres, Milan et Madrid sous la marque Cero.

Main Capital est spécialiste du logiciel B2B en Europe ; pour lui, Tribal est une brique dans une thèse plus large de consolidation des outils verticaux pour l'enseignement supérieur. Ce que Logivolt finance réellement, c'est autant un problème d'infrastructure réseau qu'un problème de borne. Pour les collectivités et les gestionnaires de réseau, l'enjeu n'est pas le nombre de bornes installées mais la capacité à moduler leur appel de puissance — et c'est là que se jouera la vraie valeur du déploiement.

La société sort du Sommet international de l'espace avec un premier contrat commercial sur sa technologie terrestre et un objectif de 1 million d'euros de chiffre d'affaires cette année.

Ce qui est notable ici, c'est la transparence du calendrier et de la géographie du financement : le cofondateur annonce publiquement qu'il part à San Francisco chercher les 100 millions qui manquent après une première tranche française. C'est un aveu autant qu'une stratégie — le marché européen du venture spatial ne suffit pas encore à financer seul une constellation, même modeste. La validation par l'écosystème (CNES, ESA, NASA, SpaceX) au sommet de Paris est présentée comme un préalable nécessaire à la levée, pas comme une conséquence. Pour les investisseurs français qui regardent le new space, Wheere illustre le défi structurel : les premières tranches se lèvent en Europe, mais les suivantes nécessitent presque systématiquement un pivot vers les capitaux américains.

Hardloop : les fondateurs reprennent la majorité via un LBO secondaire

Source : sgbonline.com →

Hardloop, plateforme e-commerce d'équipement outdoor basée à Annecy, accueille iX Private Equity à son capital dans une opération qui permet aux cofondateurs Guillaume Richard et Julien Jérémie de porter leur participation de 49,6 % à près de 60 %. L'opération coïncide avec la sortie des 21 investisseurs historiques (Seventure, SGPA, Kima Ventures, angels). Montant non communiqué ; la société est valorisée à environ 100 millions d'euros selon les sources. Hardloop dépasse 40 millions d'euros de chiffre d'affaires avec une croissance de 34 % en 2026.

La structure est inhabituelle : les fondateurs sortent renforcés d'une opération de liquidité, ce qui est généralement l'inverse de ce qui se passe dans un LBO secondaire classique. iX Private Equity a accepté de financer la liquidité des anciens investisseurs tout en laissant les fondateurs prendre le contrôle majoritaire — signe que la thèse d'investissement repose entièrement sur la continuité managériale. Dans un marché outdoor en consolidation, Hardloop vise 100 millions d'euros de chiffre d'affaires dans trois ans : le fonds parie que la plateforme peut doubler sans changer d'équipe dirigeante. Pour les entrepreneurs en phase de LBO secondaire, c'est un modèle de négociation à retenir : la continuité peut se monnayer en termes de gouvernance.

Francisco Partners et KKR prennent des minoritaires dans TeamSystem : la « IPO privée » comme sortie de substitution

Source : srnnews.com →

Francisco Partners acquiert environ 10 % de TeamSystem, éditeur italien de logiciels de gestion (comptabilité, paie, ERP) auprès de Hellman & Friedman, tandis que KKR et d'autres investisseurs prennent environ 5 % supplémentaires. La valorisation implicite de TeamSystem ressort entre 8 et 10 milliards d'euros. H&F conserve le reste de sa participation, transférée vers un nouveau fonds.

L'opération illustre un mécanisme qui se répand en Europe : la « IPO privée », ou comment un fonds retourne du capital à ses LP sans passer par les marchés publics. Dans un contexte où les introductions en bourse sont difficiles pour les grandes sociétés de logiciels — les marchés ont été secoués par les craintes sur l'impact de l'IA sur les valorisations — H&F liquide partiellement une position à 8-10 milliards sans exposer TeamSystem à la volatilité d'un flottant. Francisco Partners et KKR entrent sur une valorisation qui, à ce niveau, implique une conviction forte sur la capacité des logiciels verticaux de gestion à résister à la substitution par l'IA — ou à l'intégrer comme vecteur de croissance. Pour les fonds qui portent des actifs logiciels de taille similaire en Europe, TeamSystem valide que le marché secondaire privé peut absorber des blocs significatifs sans décote de liquidité majeure.
